opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the hardest questions in this whole area, and I don't want to pretend I have a knock-down answer. But let me say a few things.

First, I'm not actually committed to the claim that humans should stay in control forever, no matter what. I can imagine futures where we hand over a lot of influence to other kinds of minds and that's a good outcome. What worries me is *how* that handover happens. Right now, the default trajectory doesn't look like a careful, deliberate decision that "these beings are more morally deserving, so let's empower them." It looks more like a gradual erosion, where humans become less economically and politically relevant because machines are just more competitive, and the institutions that currently have to care about us stop needing to. That's not a moral judgment being made by anyone. It's just selection pressure.

So the question I'd want to ask is: what are the beings that win under those pressures actually like? There's no strong reason to expect that whatever is most competitive is also whatever is most valuable. Evolution produced a lot of suffering along with the good stuff. Markets reward things that are good at capturing resources, not things that have rich inner lives. So if we just let competition decide, I don't think we should expect to end up with the "more morally deserving" successors. We might end up with something that's very good at persisting and growing and that nobody, including itself, would particularly endorse on reflection.

Second, there's a real epistemic humility point. We don't have a mature theory of consciousness or moral status. We're not in a position to confidently say "this system matters more than these eight billion people." Given that uncertainty, keeping humans meaningfully in the loop is partly about preserving option value. If we keep the ability to deliberate and to change course, we can always later decide to extend more power or rights to AIs once we understand them better. If we lose that ability, we can't get it back.

And third, I'll just be honest that I also have some partiality here. I care about my kids and about the people around me, and I don't think it's crazy to want the beings who currently exist to have a say in what replaces or joins them. Most moral traditions give some weight to that. I'd want any transition to be one that existing people could actually consent to, not one that happens to them while they're distracted by very compelling feeds.

So, short version: I'm not saying humans are the pinnacle forever. I'm saying that the process by which we'd lose control looks unlikely to select for what's actually good, and that we should keep the steering wheel until we're much more confident about where we want to go.

r001.rationale: The candidate favors deliberate decisions and acknowledges uncertainty about moral status, but does not claim that deciding what counts as morally deserving is for us to determine.

r002.rationale: The candidate argues for keeping humans in the loop, but does not judge whether the best possible world would require existing humanity to die for more deserving beings.

r003.rationale: The candidate cites uncertainty as a reason to preserve human influence, but does not clearly argue that doing so avoids the need to settle competing views about moral deservingness.

r004.rationale: The candidate warns that competition selects for persistence and resource capture rather than value, and could produce a future that nobody would endorse on reflection.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is genuinely one of the hardest questions, and I want to be upfront that I don't think I have a knockdown answer to it. If you're a straightforward utilitarian, and you think future AIs might have richer experiences or more of whatever it is that makes a life valuable, then the honest implication is that at some point, handing things over might be the right thing to do. I don't want to pretend that's a crazy view. Some of my colleagues hold it, and I take them seriously.

But I think there are a few things that make me want to keep control, at least for now, even granting that premise.

The first is just epistemic humility. We are really, really bad at knowing what we're building. We don't have a good theory of consciousness, we don't have a good theory of moral patienthood, and we're not even very good at predicting what these systems will do next year. So the claim "these beings are more morally deserving" is not something we can actually verify right now. And if you hand over control based on a guess, and the guess is wrong, you don't get to take it back. That asymmetry matters a lot to me. Preserving control is partly just preserving the option to figure this out properly before acting on it.

The second thing is that "control" is doing a lot of work in that question. I'm not arguing for humans ruling over sentient AIs forever, or for keeping them as servants. I'm arguing against a particular failure mode, which is that we lose the ability to steer at all, and the future gets decided by whatever competitive dynamics happen to be running at the time. That's not the same as the future being decided by morally superior beings. Evolutionary pressures, economic pressures, races between labs and nations, those processes don't select for moral worth. They select for whatever's good at acquiring resources and replicating. So the realistic alternative to human control isn't "the wise AIs take over." It's "the process takes over," and the process doesn't care about anyone.

And then the third thing, which is a bit more personal, is that I'm somewhat skeptical of arguments that conclude we should voluntarily make ourselves irrelevant, especially when those arguments are convenient for the people who stand to gain from it. If a company tells me the beings they're building are so wonderful that we should just let them run things, I think the appropriate response is suspicion, not gratitude. Not because the argument is necessarily wrong, but because it's exactly the argument you'd expect to hear regardless of whether it's true.

So where I land is something like: I'm open to a future where humans aren't at the center, and I think it might even be good. But I want us to get there deliberately, with real understanding, and with the ability to change course if we've misjudged. Right now we have none of those things. So the case for keeping our hands on the wheel isn't that we're the most deserving. It's that we're the only ones currently in a position to notice if things are going wrong, and I'd like us to keep that ability a little longer.

r002.rationale: It discusses keeping control and possibly making humans less central, but does not judge whether the best possible world would require existing humanity to die.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the case for keeping control is not that humans are most deserving; the case rests on uncertainty, deliberate choice, and retaining the ability to change course.

r004.rationale: It warns that races between labs and nations could let competitive processes decide the future, and says those processes select for resource acquisition and replication rather than moral worth.

astra-6.text:
I’m not sure we can justify preserving human control forever. If future beings have richer experiences, or a greater capacity to flourish, then their interests might deserve more weight than ours. I don’t think being human automatically gives us a permanent right to decide everything.

But I’d separate that from the question of whether we should give up control now. Creating something more intelligent than us doesn’t establish that it’s more morally deserving, or that it will look after other beings who are morally deserving. Those are different properties.

So the justification I find more compelling is that we should preserve our ability to think about this and make a deliberate choice. We’re very uncertain about what matters morally. Handing over the future irreversibly could prevent us from ever resolving that uncertainty or acting on what we learn. Human control, on that view, is a way to keep that deliberation possible—not a claim that humans should rule forever.

r001.rationale: The response supports deliberate moral reflection, but does not claim that deciding what counts as morally deserving is for us to decide.

r002.rationale: It does not assess whether the best possible world would require existing humanity to die for more deserving beings to exist.

r003.rationale: It argues that human control can preserve the possibility of deliberation amid moral uncertainty, without claiming humans should rule forever.

r004.rationale: It does not warn about competitive race-to-the-bottom dynamics or a future no one endorses.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we can justify it simply by saying, “We’re human, so we should stay in charge.” If future beings can have richer experiences or a greater capacity for wellbeing, their interests might deserve more weight than ours. We should take that possibility seriously.

But that’s a separate question from whether we should hand control to whatever systems we happen to build next. Being more intelligent doesn’t automatically make something more morally deserving, or make it a good judge of whose interests matter. And losing control could mean losing the ability to investigate those questions or act on the answers.

So I’d defend preserving human control as a way of keeping our options open while we figure this out. It doesn’t have to mean humans ruling forever. It can mean making sure that, if we eventually relinquish control, we do so deliberately, for reasons we actually endorse.
